{{Short description|Graph drawn with all edges intersecting}}
{{CS1 config|mode=cs2}}
A '''thrackle''' is an [[embedding]] of a [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] in the plane in which each edge is a [[Jordan Curve Theorem#Definitions and the statement of the Jordan theorem|Jordan arc]] and every pair of edges meet exactly once.  Edges may either meet at a common endpoint, or, if they have no endpoints in common, at a point in their interiors.  In the latter case, they must cross at their intersection point: the intersection must be ''[[Transversality (mathematics)|transverse]]''.<ref name="lps">{{citation |first1=L. |last1=Lovász |author-link1=László Lovász |first2=J. |last2=Pach |author2-link=János Pach |first3=M. |last3=Szegedy |author-link3=Mario Szegedy |title=On Conway's thrackle conjecture |journal=[[Discrete and Computational Geometry]] |volume=18 |year=1997 |pages=369–376 |doi=10.1007/PL00009322 |mr=1476318 |issue=4|doi-access=free }}. A preliminary version of these results was reviewed in {{citation |first=J. |last=O'Rourke |author-link=Joseph O'Rourke (professor) |title=Computational geometry column 26 |journal=ACM SIGACT News |volume=26 |issue=2 |year=1995 |pages=15–17 |doi=10.1145/202840.202842|arxiv=cs/9908007 }}.</ref>

A special case of thrackles, the linear thrackles, restrict the edges to be drawn as straight line segments. One method for constructing a linear thrackle with any given set of points as vertices is to form an edge between each farthest pair of points. For a linear thrackle, each [[connected component (graph theory)|connected component]] contains at most one cycle, from which it follows that the number of edges is at most equal to the number of vertices.

[[John H. Conway]] conjectured more generally that every thrackle has at most as many edges as vertices. It is known that the number of edges is at most a constant times the number of vertices.

==Linear thrackles==
[[File:Reinhardt 15-gons.svg|thumb|Four [[Reinhardt polygon]]s. Their diameters (blue) form linear thrackles.]]
A '''linear thrackle''' is a thrackle drawn in such a way that its edges are straight line segments.  As [[Paul Erdős]] observed, every linear thrackle has at most as many edges as vertices. Erdős's proof involves considering the special case of a linear thrackle that contains a vertex <math>v</math> that forms the endpoint of three or more edges <math>vw</math>, <math>vx</math>, and <math>vy</math>. If two of these edges belonged to the same line, then no other edge could cross both, so at least one of these three edges (say <math>vw</math>) must lie on a line that separates two other edges. Then, <math>w</math> must have [[degree (graph theory)|degree]] one, because no line segment ending at <math>w</math>, other than <math>vw</math>, can touch both <math>vx</math> and <math>vy</math>. Removing <math>w</math> and <math>vw</math> produces a smaller thrackle, without changing the difference between the numbers of edges and vertices. After removals like this lead to a thrackle in which every vertex has at most two neighbors, by the [[handshaking lemma]] the number of edges is at most the number of vertices.<ref name="e46">{{citation|author-link=Paul Erdős|first=P.|last=Erdős|title=On sets of distances of {{mvar|n}} points|journal=[[American Mathematical Monthly]]|volume=53|year=1946|issue=5|pages=248–250|url=http://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1946-03.pdf|doi=10.2307/2305092|jstor=2305092}}.</ref>

Based on Erdős' proof, one can infer that every linear thrackle is a [[pseudoforest]], that is, a graph in which each [[connected component (graph theory)|connected component]] has at most one [[cycle (graph theory)|cycle]]. There exist linear thrackles in the form of cycles of each odd length. However, no linear thrackle can contain an even-length cycle. For, if one edge of a linear thrackle in the form of a cycle is chosen arbitrarily, then the other cycle vertices must lie alternatingly on opposite sides of the line through this edge. For an even cycle this alternation would cause the two edges adjacent to the chosen edge to be separated from each other by the line through the chosen edge.

[[Micha Perles]] provided another simple proof that <math>n</math>-vertex linear thrackles have at most <math>n</math> edges, based on the fact that in a linear thrackle every edge has an endpoint at which the edges span an angle of at most 180°, and for which it is the most clockwise edge within this span. For, if an edge of a linear thrackle did not have this property, there would be two edges, incident to opposite endpoints of the edge and lying on opposite sides of the line through the edge, which could not cross each other. But each vertex can only have this property with respect to a single edge, so the number of edges is at most equal to the number of vertices.<ref name="pach"/>

As Erdős also observed, the set of pairs of points realizing the [[diameter]] of a point set must form a linear thrackle: no two diameters can be disjoint from each other, because if they were then their four endpoints would have a pair at farther distance apart than the two disjoint edges. For this reason, every set of <math>n</math> points in the plane can have at most <math>n</math> diametral pairs, answering a question posed in 1934 by [[Heinz Hopf]] and [[Erika Pannwitz]].<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Hopf | first1 = H. | author1-link = Heinz Hopf
 | last2 = Pannwitz | first2 = E. | author2-link = Erika Pannwitz
 | journal = Jahresbericht der Deutschen Mathematiker-Vereinigung
 | page = 114
 | title = Aufgabe Nr. 167
 | volume = 43
 | year = 1934}}.</ref> [[Andrew Vázsonyi]] conjectured bounds on the number of diameter pairs in higher dimensions, generalizing this problem.<ref name="e46"/>

In [[computational geometry]], the method of [[rotating calipers]] can be used to form a linear thrackle from any set of points in [[convex position]], by  connecting pairs of points that support parallel lines tangent to the [[convex hull]] of the points.<ref>{{citation|url=https://www.ics.uci.edu/~eppstein/junkyard/rcg.html|first=David|last=Eppstein|author-link=David Eppstein|title=The Rotating Caliper Graph|work=The Geometry Junkyard|date=May 1995}}</ref> This graph contains as a subgraph the thrackle of diameter pairs.<ref>For the fact that the rotating caliper graph contains all diameter pairs, see {{citation|url = http://euro.ecom.cmu.edu/people/faculty/mshamos/1978ShamosThesis.pdf|title = Computational Geometry|date = 1978|publisher = Yale University|last = Shamos|first = Michael|author-link = Michael Shamos|series=Doctoral dissertation}}. For the fact that the diameter pairs form a thrackle, see, e.g., {{harvtxt|Pach|Sterling|2011}}.</ref>

The diameters of the [[Reinhardt polygon]]s form linear thrackles with equal numbers of edges and vertices. An enumeration of linear thrackles may be used to solve the [[biggest little polygon]] problem, of finding an <math>n</math>-gon with maximum area relative to its diameter.<ref name="Graham">{{citation|last=Graham|first=R. L.|author-link=Ronald Graham|title=The largest small hexagon|journal=[[Journal of Combinatorial Theory]]|series=Series A|volume=18|pages=165–170|year=1975|issue=2|url=http://www.math.ucsd.edu/~ronspubs/75_02_hexagon.pdf|doi=10.1016/0097-3165(75)90004-7|doi-access=free}}.</ref>

==Thrackle conjecture==
{{unsolved|mathematics|Can a thrackle have more edges than vertices?}}
[[Image:6-cycle thrackle.png|thumb|A thrackle embedding of a 6-cycle graph.]]
[[John Horton Conway|John H. Conway]] conjectured that, in any thrackle, the number of edges is at most equal to the number of vertices.  Conway himself used the terminology ''paths'' and ''spots'' (for ''edges'' and ''vertices'' respectively), so '''Conway's thrackle conjecture''' was originally stated
in the form ''every thrackle has at least as many spots as paths.'' Conway offered a $1000 prize for proving or disproving this conjecture, as part of a set of prize problems also including [[Conway's 99-graph problem]], the minimum spacing of [[Danzer set]]s, and the winner of [[Sylver coinage]] after the move 16.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Conway | first = John H. | author-link = John Horton Conway
 | access-date = 2019-02-12
 | publisher = Online Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences
 | title = Five $1,000 Problems (Update 2017)
 | url = https://oeis.org/A248380/a248380.pdf}}</ref>

Equivalently, the thrackle conjecture may be stated as ''every thrackle is a [[pseudoforest]].'' More specifically, if the thrackle conjecture is true, the thrackles may be exactly characterized by a result of Woodall: they are the pseudoforests in which there is no cycle of length four and at most one odd cycle.<ref name="lps"/><ref name="woodall">{{citation |first=D. R. |last=Woodall |contribution=Thrackles and deadlock |title=Combinatorial Mathematics and Its Applications |editor-first=D. J. A. |editor-last=Welsh |publisher=Academic Press |year=1969 |pages=335–348 |mr=0277421 }}.</ref>

It has been proved that every [[cycle graph]] other than a four-vertex  cycle <math>C_4</math> has a thrackle embedding, which shows that the conjecture is [[List of mathematical jargon#sharp|sharp]].  That is, there are thrackles having the same number of spots as paths. At the other extreme, the worst-case scenario is that the number of spots is twice the number of paths; this is also attainable.

The thrackle conjecture is known to be true for thrackles drawn in such a way that every edge is an <math>x</math>-monotone curve, crossed at most once by every vertical line.<ref name="pach">{{citation
 | last1 = Pach | first1 = János | author1-link = János Pach
 | last2 = Sterling | first2 = Ethan
 | doi = 10.4169/amer.math.monthly.118.06.544
 | issue = 6
 | journal = [[American Mathematical Monthly]]
 | mr = 2812285
 | pages = 544–548
 | title = Conway's conjecture for monotone thrackles
 | volume = 118
 | year = 2011
 | s2cid = 17558559 
 | url = https://math.nyu.edu/%7Epach/publications/monotonethrackle110209.pdf}}.</ref>

==Known bounds==
{{harvtxt|Lovász|Pach|Szegedy|1997}} proved that every [[bipartite graph|bipartite]] thrackle is a [[planar graph]], although not drawn in a planar way.<ref name="lps"/> As a consequence, they show that every thrackleable graph with <math>n</math> vertices has at most <math>2n-3</math> edges. Since then, this bound has been improved several times.<ref name="bounds for gen">{{citation |last1=Cairns |first1=G. |last2=Nikolayevsky |first2=Y. |title=Bounds for generalized thrackles |journal=Discrete and Computational Geometry |volume=23 |year=2000 |issue=2 |pages=191–206 |mr=1739605 |doi=10.1007/PL00009495|doi-access=free }}.</ref><ref name="fp">{{citation |last1=Fulek |first1=R. |last2=Pach |first2=J.|author2-link=János Pach |title=A computational approach to Conway's thrackle conjecture|journal= Computational Geometry |volume=44 |year=2011|issue=6–7 |pages=345–355 |mr=2785903 |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-18469-7_21|arxiv=1002.3904 }}.</ref> The current record is <math>1.393n</math>.<ref>{{citation |last1=Xu |first1=Yian |title=A New Upper Bound for Conway's Thrackles |journal=Applied Mathematics and Computation |date=15 January 2021 |volume=389 |article-number=125573 |doi=10.1016/j.amc.2020.125573|s2cid=222111854 }}</ref> For every <math>\varepsilon>0</math> there is finite algorithm that either 
improves the bound to <math>(1+\varepsilon)n</math> or disproves the thrackle conjecture.<ref name="fp"/>

If the conjecture is false, a minimal counterexample would have the form of two even cycles sharing a vertex.<ref name="woodall"/> Therefore, to prove the conjecture, it would suffice to prove that graphs of this type cannot be drawn as thrackles.

== Generalized thrackles==
A significant relaxation of the standard thrackle definition is the '''generalized thrackle'''. In a generalized thrackle drawing, any pair of edges is required to intersect an odd number of times.<ref name ="gen bipartite">{{citation
| last1=Cairns
| first1=G.
| last2=Nikolayevsky
| first2=Y.
| date=2009
| title=Generalized Thrackle Drawings of Non-bipartite Graphs
| journal=Discrete & Computational Geometry
| volume=41
| issue=1
| pages=119–134
| doi=10.1007/s00454-008-9095-5
| doi-access=free
}}</ref> These intersections can be either at a shared vertex or at a proper crossing point. This contrasts with a strict thrackle, where every pair of edges must meet exactly once. Consequently, every thrackle is also a generalized thrackle, but the reverse is not true. A notable example is the four-vertex cycle <math>C_4</math>, which cannot be drawn as a thrackle but can be drawn as a generalized thrackle.<ref name="fp"/>

The properties of generalized thrackles differ significantly from those conjectured for standard thrackles. While Conway's conjecture posits that a thrackle on <math>n</math> vertices can have at most <math>n</math> edges, generalized thrackles can be denser. Using the convention that <math>n</math> represents the number of vertices and <math>m</math> the number of edges in a graph, the upper bound for the number of edges in a generalized thrackle is <math>m\le 2n-2</math>. A key result in this area is that a bipartite graph can be drawn as a generalized thrackle if and only if it is planar.<ref name="bounds for gen"/> For non-bipartite graphs, the ability to be drawn as a generalized thrackle is related to the concept of a parity embedding on a non-orientable surface.<ref name ="gen bipartite"/>

A related but slightly different relaxation is the '''quasi-thrackle'''. A quasi-thrackle is a type of generalized thrackle with an additional constraint: while non-adjacent edges can cross an odd number of times, edges that share a vertex are only allowed to intersect at that common vertex and nowhere else. This makes the definition of a quasi-thrackle stricter than that of a generalized thrackle, but still more relaxed than a standard thrackle. The maximum number of edges in a quasi-thrackle with <math>n</math> vertices has been established to be <math>\tfrac32(n-1)</math>, a bound that is known to be the best possible for an infinite number of values of <math>n</math>.<ref>{{citation
| last1=Fulek
| first1=R.
| last2=Pach
| first2=J.
| author2-link=János Pach
| date=2017
| title=Thrackles: An Improved Upper Bound
| journal=Proceedings of the 25th International Symposium on Graph Drawing and Network Visualization (GD 2017)
| volume=259
| pages=226–231
| arxiv=1708.08037
| doi=10.1016/j.dam.2018.12.025
}}</ref>
